scenes.headline: How a Mac engine turns memory bandwidth into tokens
scenes.sub: Inco AI's Splash, a Metal inference engine for two Qwen models.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Ruby! Splash is an open inference engine for Macs that serves exactly two models. Here's why its speed is set by the memory bus.

scenes.text: A decode step reads 16.73 GB, one token or eight. So bandwidth sets the speed.
scenes.say: The idea: every decode step reads the same bytes, whether it emits one token or eight. So speed is bandwidth over bytes, times tokens accepted.

steps.say: A small draft model, about seven percent of the target, proposes seven tokens at once.
The twenty-seven-billion-parameter target checks them all in one pass: an anchor plus seven rows.
An exact accept test keeps what the target agrees with. Inco measured four point eight tokens per pass.
Everything, down to the recurrent state commit, is one Metal command buffer. Its bytes don't depend on how many tokens survive.

scenes.title: The speed limit
scenes.say: So a speed limit falls out of arithmetic.

parts.note: tokens accepted per pass: 4.80, published by Inco
parts.say: and multiply by tokens accepted per pass, which Inco publishes: four point eight.

scenes.title: Bandwidth for 144 tok/s
scenes.say: That checks the number going around. A hundred forty-four tokens a second needs five hundred two gigabytes a second. The forty-core M5 Max has it; the thirty-two-core doesn't.

scenes.text: Count the bytes a step reads, and the speed follows. Every kernel here exists to approach the bus, not beat it.
